analysis.one_liner: Funds nationwide testing to detect housing discrimination and boosts fair-housing enforcement grants.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2013 with 20 cosponsors, but the House Financial Services Committee never took it up, and it died without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have paid the Department of Housing and Urban Development to run a nationwide "testing" program—sending matched pairs of renters, buyers, and borrowers who differ only by race, sex, disability, or family status to see if they are treated differently. It would have raised funding for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program to $42.5 million a year, with at least 75% going to private nonprofit organizations that investigate fair-housing violations, and added grants to study the causes and effects of housing discrimination and segregation. Test results could be used as evidence in enforcement actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters, home buyers, and mortgage borrowers who face discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, disability, or national origin get a better-funded system for detecting it and building enforcement cases. Private nonprofit fair-housing organizations get a large funding increase. Veterans and military personnel, whose housing discrimination experiences were named in the grant program, and the broader public get better data on where discrimination happens.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters, buyers, and borrowers facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs HUD to conduct nationwide testing to detect and document differences in treatment of people seeking to rent, buy, or obtain or refinance a home mortgage, and to measure the prevalence of discriminatory practices across housing and lending markets.

It raises authorized funding for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program to $42.5 million a year for fiscal years 2014-2018, with at least 75% reserved for private nonprofit enforcement organizations that investigate fair-housing violations.

It authorizes $15 million a year for the HUD testing program and $5 million a year in competitive matching grants for studies of the causes and effects of housing discrimination and segregation, including on veterans and military personnel, plus pilot projects testing solutions.
Test results may be used as the basis for enforcement actions by HUD, other federal agencies, and state or local governments to remedy discriminatory housing practices.

analysis.who_pays: The federal budget bears the roughly $62 million a year in authorized spending, drawn from taxpayers. Landlords, home sellers, and mortgage lenders who treat protected groups worse would face a greater risk of being caught through testing and facing enforcement actions, since test results could be used as evidence.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes about $62 million a year in new federal spending ($15 million for testing, $42.5 million for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, $5 million for grants), which would need annual appropriations to actually flow.

Organizations receiving funds under the bill are barred from using any of it for lobbying or political advocacy, and must put up 50% matching funds (which can include in-kind donations) for the study grants—limits that reduce what grantees can do with the money.
Testing documents discrimination but does not itself change landlord or lender behavior; enforcement still depends on agencies and courts acting on the evidence.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits target a specific, concrete harm—people being denied housing or loans because of who they are—with a modest price tag, and much of the money goes to private nonprofits that investigate violations. The main honest objections are the cost and the fact that testing measures discrimination rather than eliminating it. On balance the bill's design is straightforward, with oversight requirements (tester training standards, evaluation reports, a no-lobbying restriction) built in.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to the Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a markup or a vote, so it sat there until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Al Green introduced the Housing Fairness Act of 2013 in the House on January 15, 2013, with 10 original cosponsors.
Twenty Democrats cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors.

The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on January 15, 2013, and the action history records no further action—no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote—before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, home sellers, and mortgage lenders whose differential treatment of protected groups would have been exposed by nationwide testing were spared that risk, and HUD's fair-housing funding stayed at its existing level rather than rising to the $57.5 million a year this bill authorized for enforcement and testing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords and lenders shielded from testing

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors were Democrats and there is no record of Republican support; the bill also died in a committee controlled by Republicans without any action.

industries.industry: Landlords, home sellers, and mortgage lenders
industries.note: The bill would fund nationwide paired testing of housing and mortgage markets, and test results could be used as evidence in enforcement actions. Businesses and individuals that treat protected groups worse would face a much higher chance of detection.

The bill raises the Fair Housing Initiatives Program to $42.5 million a year and reserves at least 75% for private nonprofit enforcement organizations, which also administer the testing and get first shot at the study grants. Their interest in running the program is tied to the public's interest in having discrimination detected.
The bill authorizes about $62 million a year in new spending for fiscal 2014-2018, a modest cost relative to the federal budget but a real one.
